Thanks. I always thought the 'rubber sheet' analogy was just a way for visualising gravitational attraction. Didn't realise it explains this as well.
its a way to visualize space, everything we take in can only be interpreted as 3 dimensions.

If you start with a sphere then objects collide and either fall towards the big mass or get slingshot away. Only the ones that move in the same direction don't collide stay at the same distance and you end up with a ring.

But as you go back further away, less gravity means less chance on collision because the distance between the particles/objects increase and they also move very slow. So the Oort cloud is a sphere.
Yes, very nicely explained except that it is completely wrong.

Gravity! Say 2 planets catch orbit around a star. Every time the two planets pass close enough to each other, their own gravity pulls their orbits slightly closer together. Over a lot of time, their orbits will sync up into one flat disc around the star. The more planets/objects, the faster this happens.

(Edit. Weaker/smaller planets with orbits close to opposite of the other planets may get burnt up in the sun instead.)

Blue's orbit will move slightly counterclockwise (viewer perspective) on each pass, while Red's will dramatically shift in the same direction until they are both sharing a plane.
